senses.gloss:
Aśvatīrtha
(‘place of पिल्ग्रिमगे connected with horses’)
------------------------------------------
Popular Hindu religion considers that visits to places of पिल्ग्रिमगे result in great merit as also destruction of sins. One of the minor places of पिल्ग्रिमगे (generally called ‘tīrtha’ or ‘tīrthakṣetra,’) is अश्वतीर्थ situated near Kanyākubja (the modern Kannauj in Uttar Pradesh). It is stated in the Mahābhārata (Anuśāsanaparva 4.17) that when the sage ऋचीक wanted to marry सत्यवती, the daughter of the king Gādhi (father of the famous sage विश्वामित्र) he demanded 100 white horses, with one ear black in colour, as bridal fee. ऋचीक prayed to god वरुण by whose grace the horses rose from the river गङ्गा at this point. Hence the name.
There are two more places of the same name, situated on the नर्मदा and गोदावरी rivers. The latter is said to be the place where the twin deities, the अश्विन्स्, were born (Brahmapurāṇa 89.43).

aśvinī-mudrā
(‘pose connected with the अश्विन्स्’)
------------------------------------------
Mudrās play a very significant role in the Tāntric rituals. They are generally poses of the body or of the fingers. They are said to be endowed with mystical and magical effects.
One of the 25 mudrās mentioned in the Gheraṇḍa Saṁhitā (3.77 & 78) and other such works, is the अश्विनी-मुद्रा. It consists in contracting the anus and the genital organ and dilating them again. It is said to increase the strength of the body and build up its resistance to diseases.
See also MUDRĀS.

Āśvinaśastra
(‘chant related to the अश्विन्स्’)
------------------------------------------
See ATIRĀTRA.

Āśvamedhika-parva
------------------------------------------
It is the fourteenth ‘parvan,’ branch or book of the great epic, the Mahābhārata which describes the अश्वमेध sacrifice of the king Yudhiṣṭhira
See MAHĀBHĀRATA for details.

Āśvalāyana
------------------------------------------
Each of the four वेदस् has several ‘śākhās,’ branches or recensions. The origin of these शाखास् probably lies in the fact that each of the principal sages like पैल or वैशम्पायन, who transmitted the वेदस्, had several disciples. These disciples or their successors did some editing and readjustments of the Vedic mantras to suit the needs of the rites which they performed and upon which the local culture too, sometimes, had its effect. This naturally led to the birth of these recensions.
The name of आश्वलायन is connected with the Ṛgveda as one of the authors of its शाखास्. Not much is known of this आश्वलायन except that he was the disciple of शौनक. Though one Kausalya आश्वलायन is mentioned in the Praśna Upaniṣad (1.1; 3.1) and an Aśvala in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (3.1.1) it is very difficult to establish any connection between them and this आश्वलायन. The Anuśāsanaparva (7.54) of the Mahā-bhārata mentions one आश्वलायन as belonging to the गोत्र or lineage of विश्वामित्र, another great name among the sages. Some scholars opine that he is the same आश्वलायन, the author of the Ṛgvedic recension.
The आश्वलायन recension of the Ṛgveda is almost identical with the Śākala recension except that the latter recognizes as canonical, the Vālakhilya supplementary hymn.
One or two works of आश्वलायन, out of the four attributed to him, are extant now: Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtras and Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtras.
The Āśvalāyana श्रौतसूत्रस्, which closely follows the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, consists of twelve chapters. Each chapter is further subdivided into ‘khaṇḍas’ or subsections, the total number of such khaṇḍas being 164. Each khaṇḍa is mostly in the form of a long sentence. The whole work, since it belongs to the Ṛgvedic group, deals mainly with the duties of the ‘hotṛ,’ the priest connected with the chanting of the Ṛgvedic mantras during the sacrificial rites. The sacrifices and rites dealt with in this work are: दर्शपूर्णमास, अग्न्याधान, पिण्डपितृयज्ञ, Āgrayaṇī, Kārīrīṣṭi, चातुर्मास्य, Sautrāmaṇi and सोमयाग.
The followers of this work are mostly in the southern regions of the river गोदावरी.
The Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtras consists of four chapters divided into 48 ‘kaṇḍikās’ or subsections. The topics dealt with in this work are: पाकयज्ञ, बलिहरण, and the ṣoḍaśa (Sixteen) सṁस्कारस्. Rules for the recitation of the वेदस् are also given in one of the chapters.
This work gives us the names of many ancient sages which are not found elsewhere.

aśvattha
(‘that which does not last till the next day’)
------------------------------------------
Aśvattha (Ficus religiosa) is one of the highly revered trees in popular हिन्दुइस्म्. It is said to have issued forth from इन्द्र, the king of gods. According to another version of म्य्थोलोग्य्, it is a manifestation of विष्णु. कृष्ण says in the Bhagavadgītā (10.26) that he is the अश्वत्थ among the trees. Since the gods sit under a celestial tree (vide Atharvaveda 5.3), holy men of the earth too sit under it here. Its shade is said to confer miraculous powers like understanding the language of animals or remembering former births. Childless women worship it and circumambulate it with the hope and faith of being granted children.
In the scriptures, the eternal tree of life is compared to an अश्वत्थ, with the roots in हेअवेन् and branches spread below (vide Kaṭha Upaniṣad 6.1; Maitrī Upaniṣad 6.4; Bhagavadgītā 15.1-3).
The wood of this tree was being used to prepare sacrificial vessels as also the upper अरणि (one of the two pieces of wood used for generating fire during वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्). Works of आयुर्वेद like the Suśruta Saṁhitā describe its bark, roots and fruits as being endowed with medicinal properties.

Aśvins
(‘related to the horses’)
------------------------------------------
They are twin-deities that are given an important place in the Ṛgveda. At least 50 sūktas are in praise of them. They are always described and eulogized together. Being considered as the twin sons of सूर्य (the Sun-god) and his spouse सṁज्ञा when they had assumed the horse-form, they have been described as ‘Aśvinau,’ or Aśvīni-kumāras (aśva = horse).
It is rather difficult to say what aspect of the powers of nature they represent. That they stand for night and day, or earth and sky, or मोओन् and sun, is the opinion of some scholars. There is also one view that they were originally two kings who were gradually elevated to godhood.
They are pictured as semi-darkness before dawn. They pervade this world with moisture and light. They are eternally young and handsome. In fact, they are the youngest of gods.
Their chief characteristic is that they are continuously striving to do good to others. They are expert physicians and surgeons. They know the arts of healing, rejuvenation and even plastic surgery. When supplicated, they grant children, ड़ोओद्, wealth, health and protection from enemies. Hence they are invariably invoked during the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्.
Their many exploits like granting youth to the old sage च्यवन, sight to the young उपमन्यु who had lost his eyesight, children to Mādrī, the younger queen of पाण्डु are also described in the mythological literature.
Tradition recognizes them as important teachers of आयुर्वेद, the science of health and longevity.

Aśvamedha
(‘[that in which] a horse is immolated’)
------------------------------------------
Aśvamedha is one of the most anci-ent, but major, sacrifices mentioned in the Vedic literature. It is mentioned in the Ṛgveda (1.162; 163) and described in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (13.1-5) and the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (3.8.9). It derives its name from the fact that an ‘aśva’ or a horse is made the ‘medha’ or animal for immolation. Only emperors and very powerful kings who desired sovereignty could afford to perform it. It belongs to the ‘Ahīna’ group of सोम sacrifices, i.e., सोम sacrifices in which सोम is pressed for more than one day; and, this can be from two to twelve days.
The rite begins on the 8th or 9th day of the bright half of the month of Phālguna, when the horse, which must be all white in colour with dark spots, is bound, bathed and consecrated near the fire. The animal is then let off to wander about at will for a year, guarded by an escort of four hundred armed men, including one hundred princes. The kings or chieftains of the places which the horse enters, should either accept the sovereignty of the sacrificer and pay contributions or tie up the horse and face an armed conflict. In case the challenger wins, the sacrifice will get nullified. Even the death or disease of the horse will result in the same and the sacrificer will have to restart the whole process with a new horse. Meanwhile the sacrificer is expected to perform a number of rites everyday, during the period the horse is away.
After the successful completion of the expedition and the return of the horse, the regular rites of the sacrifice commence. It is a सोम sacrifice of three days’ duration. The horse is immolated on the second day, along with a number of other victims, wild and tame, from the elephant to the bee. Before the carcass of the horse is cut up, the chief queen lies down beside it (by way of fertility spell) while an obscene dialogue between the priests and the other women of the king’s harem is enacted. Before the offering of the omentum, ‘brahmodya’ riddles (theological dialogues where questions and riddles are propounded and answered) are proposed and solved. The concluding bath (avabhṛtha-स्नान) takes place on the third day.
The sacrifice involves many subordinate rites and large quantities of gifts are given away to the priests and others.
Though long lists of kings who had performed the अश्वमेध have been given in the Vedic works already referred to, the sacrifice itself seems to have become rare even by the time of these works, since they call it as ‘utsanna’ (‘gone out of vogue’). It appears to be a curious mixture of popular religions, tribal and symbolical elements, inextricably mixed up and a remnant of a hoary past.
During the period of recorded history, Puṣyamitra Śuṅga (2nd cent. B. C.), Samudragupta (4th cent. A. D.) and some Cālukyan kings of South India seem to have performed it. The last one to perform it was जय Siṁha II of Jaipur in the 18th century.
See also AHĪNA and SOMAYĀGA.

Āśvayujī
(‘that which is performed on the आश्वयुजी day’)
------------------------------------------
The full-मोओन् day of the month of Āśvayuja or Āśvina (September-October) is called ‘āśvayujī’ and a gṛhya rite (rites mentioned in the गृह्यसूत्रस्, one of the seven pākayajñas) conducted by a householder on this day is also called by this name.
In this rite, after having adorned the होउसे, having bathed and put on clean or white garments, the householder is expected to offer cooked ड़ोओद् to पशुपति (Śiva) and also offer oblations of clarified butter to the अश्विन्स्, the twin deities.
The rite is sometimes called ‘Pṛṣātaka,’ and is performed for obtaining general prosperity. Tying of amulets of herbs on the arms is also recommended in this rite.
See also PĀKAYAJÑA.

Aśvapati
------------------------------------------
The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (5.11) mentions that six sages under the leadership of उद्दालक आरुणि, approach the king अश्वपति Kaikeya to learn Vaiśvānara-vidyā (the science concerning the Universal Self, known also as ब्रह्मन्) from him. While welcoming them he states that in his kingdom there are no thieves, misers, drunkards, ‘anāhitāgnis’ (those who have not set up consecrated Vedic fires’) as also lecherous people. He questions them individually about what they have already known and then supplements the same with his teachings.
The king of Kekaya State, the ड़थेर् of कैकेयी (the youngest of the wives of the king दशरथ of अयोध्या), was also known as अश्वपति. Whether these two were the same, it is difficult to establish. अश्वपति was reputed to have been endowed with the knowledge of all the sounds of the subhuman living beings.
The ड़थेर् of सावित्री, the well-known paragon of wifely virtues and chastity, was also an अश्वपति. He was the king of Madradeśa.

Aśvatthāman
(‘one who neighed like a horse’)
------------------------------------------
One of the great heroes of the महाभारत war, अश्वत्थामन् was the only son of द्रोणाचार्य, the teacher of the Pāṇḍava and the Kaurava princes. As soon as he was born, he is said to have neighed like a horse. Hence the name.
Though brought up in poverty he was well-trained by his ड़थेर् in the sacred lore, secular sciences and the art of war. His irascible temper often made him stray from the path of धर्म. He earned ignominy by killing the sons of द्रौपदी while they were asleep and by trying to destroy the baby परीक्षित् in the womb of उत्तरा, the wife of अभिमन्यु and the future heir to the empire. He was punished by भीम, the second of the Pāṇḍavas and cursed by Śrī कृष्ण to suffer from serious diseases for a very long time. Though a little odd, he has been reckoned as one of seven ‘Cirañjīvins’ or ‘those who live forever.’

Aśvinī
(‘equestrian’)
------------------------------------------
It is the very first of the twentyseven nakṣatras or constellations of स्तर्स् listed by the Hindu अस्त्रोनोम्य्. It is said to be associated with the ‘Aśvins,’ the twin Vedic deities, the physicians of the gods in हेअवेन्. It is identified with the स्तर्स् beta and gamma Arietis. In Hindu अस्त्रोलोग्य् its influence is considered beneficent.
See also NAKṢATRA.
